units.candidate_text: You still want suffering to end. Metta also helps you hold that wish without becoming desperate or afraid you’ll fail.

Nine days of the intense part have already passed by the time the kindness arrives. I’d want it available when trauma surfaces. That skips the Buddha’s kindness-first approach as I understand it: he taught that kindness was necessary to prepare the mind for real nibbana meditation.
I take the possibility of starting with metta seriously, and Oliver’s experience is part of why. That’s what I’m including it for. You don’t have to treat his experience as a template for your own.

If you already know that sitting with intense internal material can destabilize you, there are gentler ways into meditation. I’d begin with metta and see how that felt before deciding whether I wanted more. If it felt steady and I was still interested, I might explore trauma-informed mindfulness or Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction with a therapist. A retreat would still depend on whether I wanted one after that. Before going, I’d want to ask Plum Village, or whichever retreat I was considering: what happens if I start destabilizing? Can I pause the practice as an ordinary part of being there?
You get to decide how your practice takes shape. A trauma-informed retreat should respect that, without making the decision to keep practicing a test of character.
You can skip these if you don’t need them; some are rough to read. They’re anecdotes, so they can’t tell us how often any of this happens.
